text: This lesson closes chapter one by walking Northbeam's support assistant through four real growth stages, end to end -- tying together load, cost, and latency budgets, capacity planning, and high-availability design into one continuous story instead of four separate ideas. Treat this as a rehearsal for the kind of 'how would you have handled this' conversation a real architecture review, or a Staff or Principal interview, actually puts in front of you.

Stage one is the pilot: about a hundred daily users, a single vector database instance, one LLM provider, one application server, all in one region. This is the right architecture for this stage -- anything more elaborate would be solving problems that don't exist yet. Stage two is department rollout, at roughly five thousand daily users, where cost and latency budgeting becomes necessary for the first time. Stage three is company-wide, at fifty thousand users, where capacity planning becomes load-bearing. And stage four is public-facing, at a million users, where high-availability design finally earns its cost.

At stage two, the team runs the per-request cost math and discovers their system prompt has grown bloated over months of ad-hoc tweaks, and sets an explicit latency budget table because agents are complaining the tool feels slow with no specific number attached. The fix here is entirely about discipline -- trimming the prompt, setting budgets -- not new infrastructure. Reaching for multi-region complexity at this stage would be solving stage four's problem three stages too early.

At stage three, the team runs a growth forecast and discovers the current vector database tier will hit its ceiling in a projected seven months -- and, critically, that migrating to a higher tier takes three months of real engineering work. That lead-time math is what actually drives the roadmap decision, not the raw ceiling date, so the team starts the migration at month four, with comfortable margin, instead of reacting to a capacity incident at month seven.

At stage four, leadership decides to expose a public-facing version of the assistant directly to customers -- a different risk profile, where an outage now means real customer-facing downtime with reputational and revenue consequences. A single region's five hundred twenty-five minutes a year of downtime, tolerable for an internal tool, is no longer acceptable. The team moves to an active-active multi-region deployment, specifically audits for shared dependencies like a shared model API account or auth service that would silently break the independence assumption, and adds a defined graceful-degradation mode -- retrieval-only results -- for when the LLM provider is unavailable everywhere at once.

Notice the pattern: multi-region deployment is correct and necessary at stage four, and would have been wasteful over-engineering at stage one. Capacity forecasting is essential at stage three and premature at stage one. This is the actual skill a real interview or architecture review tests -- not whether you know what multi-region deployment is, but whether you know when it's the right call, and can say why it would have been wrong earlier. Reaching for the most sophisticated-sounding architecture at every stage reads as inexperience, not expertise.
Next, chapter two: architecture decision records -- the documents that make a decision like this actually stick, instead of getting re-litigated every time.
